# Multi-view projection
Also called: Multi-view voxelization, 3-axis projection voxelization

## Overview
Multi-view projection voxelization generates a 3D voxel representation of a scene by rasterizing geometry from multiple orthogonal viewing directions, typically aligned with the principal axes. It solves the problem of geometric holes, cracks, and missing surface data that occur when voxelizing from a single viewpoint, ensuring robust coverage for subsequent volume rendering or ray tracing. It differs from single-view methods by explicitly handling degenerate cases where triangles are parallel to the viewing direction, and from compute-shader methods by relying on standard rasterization pipelines to project geometry into intermediate buffers.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of decomposing 3D occupancy into a union of 2D projections. The general workflow involves:
1.  **Axis Selection:** Defining a set of viewing directions, typically the three principal axes ($X, Y, Z$) or a subset thereof.
2.  **Projection:** Transforming scene geometry (triangles) into clip space using orthographic or perspective projection matrices aligned with these axes.
3.  **Rasterization:** Rasterizing the projected geometry into 2D buffers (sheet buffers) or directly into a 3D texture.
4.  **Accumulation:** Combining the results from all views. This is often done via union semantics (occupancy) or atomic accumulation (counting overlaps) to resolve conflicts and fill gaps.

Key mathematical constraint: The projection must handle the "thinness" of triangles. When a triangle's normal is parallel to the viewing direction, its 2D projection collapses to a line or point, leading to missing voxels. Shared principles include strategies to mitigate this, such as selecting the dominant axis for projection or using multiple views to ensure at least one view sees the triangle face-on.

## Subtopics

### [Single 2D Projection Voxelization](3482-single-2d-projection-voxelization.md)
A specialized variant that uses only a single 2D orthographic projection along the dominant axis of a triangle's normal to produce a 6-separating (tunnel-free) voxelization. It leverages the "thinness" property to avoid the cost of multi-view projections. Unlike [Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization](3892-orthographic-multi-view-voxelization.md) which projects along all three axes, this approach relies on the fact that for pixels containing the triangle's center, the dominant axis projection is sufficient to determine the unique voxel, while edge cases are resolved via crosshair-segment intersection tests. It is chosen when computational resources are limited and the geometry consists of isolated planar triangles where 6-connectivity is critical. See [Single 2D Projection Voxelization](3482-single-2d-projection-voxelization.md).

### [Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization](3892-orthographic-multi-view-voxelization.md)
The standard multi-view approach that rasterizes scene geometry into a 3D voxel grid using three orthographic cameras aligned with the scene's bounding box axes ($X, Y, Z$). It builds on [Multi-view projection](5937-multi-view-projection.md) by explicitly managing three directional sheet buffers to synthesize a final volume, avoiding the degenerate rasterization artifacts that occur when triangles are parallel to the viewing direction. Unlike [Single 2D Projection Voxelization](3482-single-2d-projection-voxelization.md), which suffers from missing geometry on surfaces parallel to the single view axis, this method ensures robust coverage through union semantics across all three axes. It is chosen for general-purpose voxelization where geometric completeness is required. See [Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization](3892-orthographic-multi-view-voxelization.md).

### [Volumetric Representation via Depth Map Registration](6435-volumetric-representation-via-depth-map-registration.md)
A method that constructs a 3D volume from a set of multi-view images by registering estimated depth maps into a voxel grid. It specifically handles non-Lambertian reflections by using individual minimum cost per view rather than a global threshold. It represents scene geometry as a sparse voxel cloud where voxel values indicate the number of views mapping to that location, serving as the initialization phase for subsequent volume refinement and color selection. It is chosen when the input is a set of images/depth maps rather than a triangle mesh. See [Volumetric Representation via Depth Map Registration](6435-volumetric-representation-via-depth-map-registration.md).

#### 3-Pass Voxelization
**Definition**
A voxelization approach that fixes cracks and missing data in the voxel grid by voxelizing the scene from each of the 3 major axes, requiring 3 render passes [S1, unofficial].

**Steps**
For each of the 3 major axes, multiply the clip-space projection matrix by a rotation matrix corresponding to that axis to generate fragments from that view-axis [S1, unofficial]. Use the voxel-space projection matrix without multiplying it by the rotation matrix, as it already maps all values properly [S1, unofficial].

**Pitfalls**
Requires 3 render calls per rendered object, which becomes expensive as models become more complex [S1, unofficial]. If optimizing by separating dynamic and static objects, the voxel grid of dynamic objects must be cleared every frame, requiring separate voxel grids for dynamic and static objects [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of multi-view voxelization originated as a solution to the "cracking" artifacts inherent in single-pass rasterization-based voxelization. Early real-time voxel global illumination systems identified that voxelizing from a single direction leads to missing data where triangles are edge-on to the camera [S1, unofficial]. The 3-pass approach was introduced to ensure that every surface is viewed face-on by at least one of the three principal axes, thereby guaranteeing full coverage. This technique is widely used in real-time ray tracing pipelines, particularly for voxel cone tracing and global illumination, where a complete and watertight voxel representation is necessary to prevent light leaks and artifacts.
